description: Canonical glossary of Victorian street-trade slang from the Mayhew 1851 extract. Every entry cites the source.txt line(s) where the term is introduced or defined. Pull full context via /api/source?start=&end=.

entries.definition: The copper (and other metal) scrap scavenged from the Thames sewers by sewer-hunters. More generally, anything of value pulled from the underground. Mayhew: "a word more particularly applied by them to anything made of copper."
entries.etymology: Origin disputed; likely cant term tied to the trade itself — the hunters are "toshers" because what they bring up is "tosh."

entries.definition: Sewer-hunters. Men who work the Thames-side sewer outlets at low tide in long greasy velveteen coats, with eight-foot iron-hooked poles, hunting for copper, iron, rope, bone, and coin. Also call themselves shore-men or shore-workers.
Dogs' dung, collected from London streets and sold to Bermondsey tanyards for use in dressing leather (the alkaline ammonia in canine faeces was used to purify the grain of morocco and kid).
entries.etymology: Ironic trade-term — what the tanners 'purify' the leather with. Mayhew parenthesises it as "(or dogs'-dung)" when first introduced at line 16.

entries.definition: Older female rag-gatherers who added the collecting of 'pure' to their original trade. Mayhew notes the term "signifies properly gatherers of rags."
entries.etymology: Cant word for low-class women, esp. rag-pickers.

entries.definition: Winter night-asylums for the destitute — sheds and barns strewn with straw, opened in the cold months to house those who would otherwise sleep in the street. Close around the beginning of April.
entries.etymology: Literal — yards floored with straw for sleeping on.

entries.definition: Seasonal country labourers who winter in London as street-finders, returning to the country in April to work the harvest.
entries.etymology: From 'to tramp' — the casual walking-labour they do between cities and seasons.

entries.definition: The sewer-hunters' self-designation — they prefer it to 'toshers'. Also 'shore-workers'. Named for the Thames foreshore where they enter the sewer outlets at low tide.
entries.etymology: Literal — 'shore' as in the Thames foreshore.

entries.definition: A self-employed dredgerman (or, in the dust trade, a small-scale contractor) — working on his own account rather than for a larger licensed trader.
entries.etymology: Contrast to the licensed London 'Masters' of the trade.

entries.definition: The coarser portion of sifted house-dust (as opposed to 'soil', the fine portion). Sold to brick-makers for firing bricks — the buried cinders in the dust ignite when the brick is baked.
entries.etymology: Variant spelling of 'breeze' — cinder/ash residue; same root as the wind.

entries.definition: Unlicensed dust collectors — 'small men' who operate outside the contracted London parish system, usually collecting door-to-door for small cash payments.
entries.etymology: Literal — they 'run' the rounds rather than holding a licensed pitch.

entries.definition: The Paris equivalent of London bone-grubbers and rag-gatherers, organised into a ranked fraternity with class-ranked meeting rooms and an annual banquet. Invoked by Mayhew as a comparative case.
